title: Layout and Formatting in Informational Writing
keyIdea: Layout devices help a reader find their way around an information text. A heading names the whole topic and a sub-heading names one section in a few words. Bullet points list separate items, a numbered list shows steps in order, a table compares several things on the same features, and columns put two sets of points side by side. Ideas linked by because and so still belong in a paragraph.

kid: Readers of a guide or a leaflet rarely read every word. They scan for the part they need. Layout devices help them do that. A heading tells them the topic. Sub-headings split the text into sections, and each one names its section in a few words, like Food or Winter sleep.

Pick the device that fits the content. Use bullet points for separate items in no set order, such as a kit list. Use a numbered list for steps that must happen in order. If you swap two steps, the reader goes wrong, so number them.

Use a table when you compare several things on the same features. Row headers go down the side and column headers go across the top. Each fact sits where its row and column meet, written as a short note. Columns put two sets of points side by side, such as Do and Don't.

Some writing should stay as a paragraph. If you explain why something happens, your ideas are joined by because and so. Bullets would break those links. Good layout is not decoration. Each device has a job: helping the reader find, follow or compare.
adult: This is the Year 6 writing objective in England's national curriculum. Pupils use organisational and presentational devices to structure text and guide the reader. English Appendix 2 lists layout devices for Year 6: headings, sub-headings, columns, bullets and tables. In the US, Common Core W.4.2a and W.5.2a ask pupils to group related information in sections and include formatting such as headings when it aids understanding.

Key terms: layout device, organisational device, presentational device, heading, sub-heading, bullet point, numbered list, table, row header, column header, cell and column. The test for any device is what the reader needs to do: find a section, follow steps, scan items or compare features.

Common mistakes: sub-headings that are whole sentences or too vague to help, such as More facts. Bullets used for steps where order matters. Tables with no headers, or with full sentences crammed into cells. A careful writer also avoids bullet-pointing an explanation, which strips out the because and so that carry the reasoning.

In the lab your learner drags sub-headings onto three sections of a hedgehog guide, with a vague label and a full sentence as decoys. They sort five pieces of content into bullets, numbers, a table or a paragraph, and file six facts into a table using its headers. Then they swipe tips into Do and Don't columns and fix a leaflet with three layout slips.

familyTip: Pick up a leaflet, a recipe or a museum guide together. Ask your learner to point out each layout device and say what job it does for the reader. Then ask them to find one place where the layout could work better, and how they would change it.

visual.caption: Which layout device fits each piece of content? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: What to pack: hat, water, map, snack

How to plant a seed, step by step

lab.caption: Flagship lab: place sub-headings, pick the right device, build a table from its headers, sort tips into columns, and fix a leaflet's layout slips.

practice.prompt: You are writing how to make a bird feeder. The steps must be done in order. Which device fits?
choices: A numbered list
Bullet points
A table
practice.hint: Ask: does the order of the points matter to the reader?
practice.explain: The order matters, so number the steps. Bullet points suggest the items could come in any order.

practice.prompt: A table compares {a} animals on {b} features. Each animal has a row and each feature has a column. How many cells hold facts, not counting the headers?
practice.hint: Each animal row has one fact cell for every feature column.
practice.explain: {a} rows times {b} columns gives {=a*b} fact cells. Each fact sits where its row and its column meet.

practice.prompt: Which is the best sub-heading for a section about where owls nest?
choices: Nesting places
Owls are birds that hunt mostly at night
Other information
practice.hint: A sub-heading is a short label that names what this section is about.
practice.explain: Nesting places names the section in two words. The long sentence is not a label, and Other information does not tell the reader anything.

practice.prompt: A leaflet has one main heading and {n} sections. Each section gets its own sub-heading. How many headings and sub-headings are there in all?
practice.hint: Count one sub-heading per section, then add the main heading.
practice.explain: {n} sub-headings plus 1 main heading makes {=n+1}. The heading names the topic and each sub-heading names one section.

pool.prompt: You compare the speed, food and habitat of four big cats. Which device fits best?
choices: A table
A numbered list
One long paragraph
pool.hint: Are you comparing several things on the same features?
pool.explain: A table lines up the same features for all four cats, so the reader can compare down a column.

pool.prompt: Why do information texts use sub-headings?
choices: So readers can find the section they need
To make the text longer
Because every page must have them
pool.hint: Think about how people use a guide: do they read every word?
pool.explain: Readers scan. Sub-headings name each section, so they can jump to the part they need.

pool.prompt: Which content should stay as a paragraph?
choices: An explanation of why volcanoes erupt
A list of things to bring on a trip
The steps to tie a knot
pool.hint: Look for ideas that are joined by because and so.
pool.explain: An explanation links causes and effects with because and so. Bullets would break those links.

pool.prompt: A table about pets has no column headers. What goes wrong?
choices: The reader cannot tell what each column means
Nothing, the facts are still there
The rows are in the wrong order
pool.hint: How does a reader know what a column of facts is about?
pool.explain: Column headers name what each column holds. Without them the reader has to guess what the facts mean.

pool.prompt: A writer puts these as bullet points: mix the flour, bake for 20 minutes, grease the tin. What is the slip?
choices: They are steps in order, so they should be numbered
Bullets should be full paragraphs
They need a table
pool.hint: Does the reader need to do these in a set order?
pool.explain: Recipe steps happen in order, so a numbered list fits. Here the tin must be greased before baking, and numbers make that clear.

pool.prompt: A safety poster lists things to do and things not to do. Which layout helps the reader most?
choices: Two columns headed Do and Don't
One paragraph with every tip
A numbered list of all the tips
pool.hint: Which layout lets the reader see the two sets side by side?
pool.explain: Two headed columns keep the sets apart and side by side, so the reader can see at once what to do and what to avoid.

pool.prompt: A table compares {a} rivers on length, source and mouth. It also has one header row. How many rows does the table have in all?
pool.hint: One row for each river, plus the header row across the top.
pool.explain: {a} river rows plus 1 header row is {=a+1} rows. The header row names the columns: length, source and mouth.

pool.prompt: Which is a well-written cell in a table about planets, under the column Moons?
choices: Mars has two small moons called Phobos and Deimos.
Moons
pool.hint: Table cells hold short notes. The headers already say what the cell is about.
pool.explain: The row says Mars and the column says Moons, so the cell only needs 2. Full sentences make tables slow to scan.

pool.prompt: A guide has {n} sections, each with a sub-heading. A reader wants the last section. Without sub-headings they read every section to find it. How many sections do they read?
pool.hint: With no labels the reader has to check each section in turn.
pool.explain: They check all {=n} sections. A sub-heading on each one lets them jump straight to the last section instead.
